body:
You might want to do a bit more validate given what OpenXR itself seems to be using:
```

include/openxr/openxr.h
29:#define XR_CURRENT_API_VERSION XR_MAKE_VERSION(1, 1, 54)
32:#define XR_API_VERSION_1_0 XR_MAKE_VERSION(1, 0, XR_VERSION_PATCH(XR_CURRENT_API_VERSION))
1924:#define XR_API_VERSION_1_1 XR_MAKE_VERSION(1, 1, XR_VERSION_PATCH(XR_CURRENT_API_VERSION))
```

So the third int should go through `XR_VERSION_PATCH` (which doesn't seem to do anything relevant but I'm no Khronos dev :P), but most importantly I think the first two can only be `1.0` or `1.1`, at least until we upgrade to some OpenXR 1.2.x SDK.

And given how `XR_API_VERSION_1_0` and `XR_API_VERSION_1_1` are defined, you might want to document that users can choose to target OpenXR 1.0 even with the latest SDK by inputting `1.0.54` (which is not a tagged release, but seems to be the 1.1.54 release being able to still function as OpenXR 1.0 SDK with patch 54 changes.

body:
```suggestion
			Optionally sets a specific API version of OpenXR to initialize in [code]major.minor.patch[/code] notation. [code]major.minor[/code] can be [code]1.0[/code] or [code]1.1[/code] depending on the desired OpenXR version to target, and [code]patch[/code] matches a given SDK release (for example [code]1.1.54[/code]). Some XR runtimes gate old behavior behind version checks. This is non-standard OpenXR behavior.
```

Yeah that makes sense.

It's an advanced setting for a niche issue so in the grand scheme of things, I'm fine if we don't go too deep in the validation logic, as long as the docs are clear about what format is expected.

The main question I suppose is what happens if you pass invalid values and we don't validate (e.g. `2.0.100`).
Does it fail with a cryptic error or does OpenXR actually report something meaningful that would let users understand their config mistake?

> It's an advanced setting for a niche issue so in the grand scheme of things, I'm fine if we don't go too deep in the validation logic, as long as the docs are clear about what format is expected.

Yeah, I agree and I'd also be fine with not adding more validation logic

> Does it fail with a cryptic error or does OpenXR actually report something meaningful that would let users understand their config mistake?

Users should get a message like `Failed to create XR instance [XR_ERROR_API_VERSION_UNSUPPORTED]` in the logs

And if they have verbose stdout enable, this PR adds a print showing that a custom version is being tried. So, those two things in a row should make things fairly clear
Or, `target_api_version`? OpenXR isn't really an SDK, at least in my mind
Sounds good, then I think this part is fine as is, with my suggested documentation changes sufficient to make it clear.

The OpenXR repo does call itself an SDK: https://github.com/KhronosGroup/OpenXR-SDK
But yeah I'm fine with API too. And on second thought I think Bastiaan used `custom` because this is only used if set, while starting with `target` may sound like it needs to be filled.

In my mind "API" is the `major.minor` part, i.e. OpenXR 1.0 vs OpenXR 1.1.
And the "patch" version is the version of the headers and loader that implements (apparently) both API versions.

So... maybe `custom_version` isn't the worst option, if neither `api` nor `sdk` would be fully accurate additional specifiers.

I'm also leaning toward calling this either `target_sdk_version` or `target_api_version`, and prepopulating with the default version the engine is using.
This would match the approach we use for Android where the default min and target SDK are prepopulated in similar fields but we allow users to change them (with appropriate validation logic) as they desire.

body:
```suggestion
		<member name="xr/openxr/target_sdk_version" type="String" setter="" getter="" default=""1.1.54"">
			Specifies the SDK version of OpenXR to initialize in [code]major.minor.patch[/code] notation. [code]major.minor[/code] can be [code]1.0[/code] or [code]1.1[/code] depending on the desired OpenXR version to target, and [code]patch[/code] matches a given SDK release (for example [code]1.1.54[/code]).
```

I'm not sure about pre-populating it.

Keeping it blank makes it easy to distinguish between "the developer didn't set it" (in which case we want both our default version and the OpenXR 1.0 fallback) and "the developer really specifically wants this version" (in which case we shouldn't try to fallback because we want this one).

I think this logic in the PR already covers it:
```
if (result == XR_ERROR_API_VERSION_UNSUPPORTED && init_version == XR_API_VERSION_1_1) {
```

If we prepopulate and the version we retrieve from the field matches our default, then we apply the fallback if init fails, otherwise we don't as the current logic does.

Asides from the field name and description, I don't think pre-populate should change any of the current logic, so it's more of a matter of how this presented to the end user. I think another advantage is that we have a location that explicitly describe which version of OpenXR the engine is using.. I don't think we show that information currently.

I thought about this (at least to put a placeholder with the curent OpenXR version), but that would imply including OpenXR in main.cpp and that's a no-no.

So the definition of those settings should be moved someplace else (not sure why they're in main and not in the OpenXR module).

I can't remember exactly why but they started life in the OpenXR module. Either I was told to move them, or they were moved during a cleanup by someone else, I'm not sure. Might be worth a git blame.

Personally I think it makes more sense to have them in the module so they can also be compiled out if OpenXR is not included.

We also have to keep in mind that the behaviour we're trying to get here is not an OpenXR standard. We're doing this purely to deal with the behavior in Metas XR runtime. It's why I marked this as an advanced setting so people don't normally see it, and I'm personally partial to leaving it empty unless you have a reason to put something in there.

Btw, Akien, the patch number remaining in sync with OpenXR 1.0 and 1.1 is a standard, I was confused by this as well. It seems they do the same with Vulkan. They reset the patch number when the major version changes, so once OpenXR 2.0 releases, we're back at patch 0.
